newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea union leader in no mood for compromise.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea union leader in no mood for compromise.

text.p: South Korean union leader Kwon Young-kil said on Sunday striking workers would not compromise even though the government appeared to be offering a peaceful solution to a three-week-old industrial crisis.

Speaking outside a makeshift tent pitched on the grounds of Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral where he and six other union leaders have sought sanctuary, Kwon said public support for the strikers was increasing.

About 2,000 workers later held a rally on the cathedral grounds to protest against a controversial new labour law which allows firms to lay off workers and hire temporary staff to break strikes, shattering a jobs-for-life labour tradition.
Thousands of riot police prevented more workers from getting near the grounds, witnesses said. There were no incidents.
Workers wielding iron bars have manned entry points to the sacred grounds of the gothic cathedral around-the-clock to block prosecutors from handing arrest warrants to the seven unionists.
"We will not accept the law...The public and the opposition parties will also not accept the law," said Kwon, the president of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.
"If the law comes into effect, it will destroy 12 million workers' lives and the public life," he said in an interview.

South Korea's ruling party chief Lee Hong-koo, in an apparent attempt to avoid more confrontation, challenged union leaders on Saturday to a televised debate over the law, which has sparked three weeks of wildcat strikes across the nation and growing international criticism.
Kwon, who said worker resolve was undiminished, rejected the offer, which he called a "propaganda ploy".
The main union body, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, has also brushed aside the offer to discuss the law.

Kwon said his 500,000-member union would strike on Wednesday if the law had not been scrapped. That would coincide with a call by the federation, which has 1.2 million members, to down tools for two days starting on Tuesday in what would be the biggest strike in South Korea's history.

Kwon claimed private research institutes had figures that showed public support for the strikers had risen to 64 percent from 55 percent since President Kim Young-sam took a tough stance against the strikes in a New Year press briefing.
A copy of the figures was not immediately available.
Public opinion is seen as crucial in the stoppages, which have closed car plants and disrupted hospitals.

South Korean unions denounce the legislation as an "evil law", and international labour organisations have said it is even harsher than the law it replaced. Seoul officials say the law is needed to rescue the economy from a worrying downturn.
Earlier on Sunday, Kwon and other union leaders met representatives of international labour groups.
As they talked, unperturbed churchgoers picked their way through piles of rocks, firewood used by strikers to keep warm and other debris on their way to morning mass.
Guy Ryder, who heads the Geneva office of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, said if the union leaders were arrested international pressure on Seoul would increase.

On Saturday, about 20,000 workers calling for the resignation of President Kim clashed with riot police in the most violent street protests since the labour bill was rammed through parliament on December 26.
